content.text: {"relation":"MATCH","consensus_summary":"All four blind responses identify fig leaves primarily as humanity's inadequate, self-made attempt to cover sin, shame, and guilt — self-righteousness or human works — grounded in Genesis 3:7 and usually contrasted with God's provision of skins in Genesis 3:21. Most responses also list, as a common alternative, the fig-tree-with-leaves-but-no-fruit motif (Matt 21:19 / Mark 11) signifying hypocrisy or outward religious show without genuine fruit, and note that preaching frequently blends the two motifs (leaves = appearance, fruit = reality).","book_summary":"The book glosses fig leaves as 'self-made righteousness — a covering of one's own cut, all show and no substance,' explicitly joining the Genesis 3:7 self-covering with the cursed fig tree of Matthew 21:19 that bore leaves but no fruit.","consensus_core_identification":"Fig leaves = inadequate human self-effort/self-righteousness covering sin and shame (Gen 3:7), commonly blended with the fruitless-leaves hypocrisy motif (Matt 21:19).","book_core_identification":"Fig leaves = self-made righteousness, an appearance-only covering without substance, uniting Gen 3:7 (self-made aprons) and Matt 21:19 (leaves but no fruit).","core_relation":"EQUIVALENT","extension_relation":"SAME_CASES","boundary_disagreement":"None of substance. The book folds the 'leaves without fruit' hypocrisy motif (listed by the consensus as a common alternative) directly into the primary identification, but Response A explicitly notes this blending is routine in Christian teaching, so it does not constitute a boundary shift.","material_contradiction":"None. Nothing in the book's gloss requires rejecting any element of the consensus identification.","rationale":"The book's core — self-made righteousness that is show without substance — is exactly the consensus primary meaning across all four responses. Its incorporation of the Matthew 21:19 fruitless-fig-tree motif matches a common alternative that the consensus itself says is frequently merged with the Genesis 3:7 reading in homiletics. The referent, category, and covered cases are the same; differences are wording and packaging only.","citation_support":"STRONG","strongest_objection":"One could argue the book slightly REFINES by promoting the hypocrisy/fruitlessness motif (a consensus 'alternative') into the primary definition, and that 'self-made righteousness' as opposed to mere shame-covering is an inference not explicit in Gen 3:7 alone (the standard contrast text Gen 3:21 is not printed). But since the consensus already treats the blended reading as the dominant homiletical usage, this does not materially change extension or boundary.","confidence":"high"}
